# Phase 3 reconciliation fixtures

Inputs and expected outputs for `prov-2026-4c49ca46`: what Phase 3 does when an
authorized path already exists.

Each case directory holds `existing` (the file on disk), `template` (the file
template **as rendered**, never the template source), and — for a case that
applies — `expected`. A case that halts has no `expected`; `cases.json` carries
the diagnostic it must produce instead.

**`comment_prefix` is per case, not per corpus.** An earlier revision carried one
prefix for the whole file, which would have meant editing the corpus's shape to
add a second language — the exact smell the no-target-knowledge principle exists
to catch. Cases span `#`, `//` and `;;` today, and a fourth prefix needs a case
and nothing else.

These are internal fixtures rather than a published surface, which is why they
live under `testdata/` and not beside `conformance/`. The marker corpus is
published because a third party writes that format; nothing outside Sedum
implements this.

## Where the inputs come from

Nothing here is hand-written to make a point.

The Rails inputs are real: `rails-new-routes` is `config/routes.rb` from
`rails _7.2.3_ new --api`, and the `rails-generate-*` cases are rendered from
railties' own `controller.rb.tt`. The Go and Cairn inputs are generated by Sedum
from the packages in this repository, then evolved by adding an anchor to the
template and regenerating. Every rendered template comes from
`grow --stop-after files`.

## Languages, and where the coverage is thin

The mechanism reads no language. It compares lines, treats a line as structural
unless it is blank or starts with the package's declared `comment_prefix`, and
constrains the edit script to insertions. No rule below names Ruby, Go, `end`,
`}`, `private`, or `package`.

Evidence for that is deliberately not all Ruby:

| prefix | cases | covers |
|---|---|---|
| `#` | 11 | adoption, evolution, empty, halts |
| `//` | 4 | evolution, empty, halt, no-op |
| `;;` | 2 | evolution, empty |

`go-evolution` is the one to read next to `evolution-anchor-and-code`. Both are
an anchor arriving with the code it needs — `private` in Ruby, `func init() { }`
in Go — and Go is the harder of the two, because `}` repeats far more than `end`
does.

**Adoption evidence is Ruby-only, and that is a gap rather than a decision.** The
adoption cases need a file some *other* tool wrote, and Rails is the one stack
here with a real generator (`rails new`, `rails generate`) to produce authentic
input. Constructing a plausible Go file by hand would be evidence about my
imagination rather than about the mechanism. A real Go adoption case should be
added when there is a genuine artifact to take it from.

## What each case is evidence for

`cases.json` carries a `why` per case. Two are worth knowing before reading the
data:

- **`rails-generate-bare` applies and `rails-generate-actions` halts.** The
  boundary is not "controller templates cannot be adopted" — an empty generated
  controller adopts exactly, one carrying hand-written actions does not.
- **`private-with-method` halts because of the method, not the keyword.**
  `private-empty` is the same file without it, and applies.

## Expected outputs state required behaviour

They are not transcripts of a prototype. Two cases record behaviour the spike
this record was written from does not yet produce, and the fixtures are right:
`private-empty` carries a blank line between the `actions` anchor and `private`,
and `cairn-evolution` expects the template verbatim rather than the spike's
doubled blank line. Both are the same defect — bookkeeping at the boundary of a
gap — and the implementation has to meet the fixture, not the other way round.
